task: Write one sentence of your own using the word decry. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know decry should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Every generation of grandparents finds something new to decry — this year it is wireless earbuds at the dinner table.
To grumble is to mutter your discontent under your breath; to decry is to lift the same complaint into the open, where everyone can hear it.
Revile goes further than decry: the critic who decries a policy attacks the policy, while the one who reviles it heaps loathing on it — and often on whoever wrote it.

To criticize is the plain, all-purpose word for finding fault, in any setting and at any volume — a margin note criticizes as quietly as a protest sign shouts. Decry narrows it: the fault-finding is public and raised-voice, aimed at a practice, and kept up where everyone can hear.

To bemoan something is to voice sorrow over it — hands wrung, the loss mourned aloud — with blame a distant second or missing entirely. Decry runs the other way: blame first, raised in public against a target that has earned the disapproval.

News of the stadium's demolition was met with a public outcry that filled three council meetings.
Decry means to criticize openly.

The transit app's update dropped the night map, and the city's night shift wasted no time: hundreds of nurses and warehouse crews flooded the developer's message boards and the morning call-in shows to decry an update that treated riders asleep by midnight as the only riders who mattered.
Decry is the exact word because the criticism is open and aimed at a practice: the workers raise a public cry against the update itself.
Grumbling in a break room would be private; mourning the old map would be mere sadness.
To decry is to say out loud, where everyone can hear, that a thing deserves disapproval — and to keep saying it.
Decry is the press-conference word for criticizing openly — groups decry policies, practices, and trends, at volume and in public.
Its unit-mate denounce swings harder: to decry a rule is to keep up the cry against it; to denounce it is to pass official public judgment on it, often in a single thunderclap of a statement.
For quiet, sorrowing disapproval, bemoan is nearer the mark.

When the daguerreotype reached Paris in 1839, the painting establishment did not respond quietly.
Academy lecturers took to public halls to decry the new machine portraits, calling them soulless chemistry and a menace to art itself.
Pamphlets followed, then open letters in the journals, the same charges repeated season after season for a decade.
What is striking now is how public the campaign stayed.
Private doubts existed, but the fight was carried out at podiums and in print, where everyone could follow it.
Painters kept painting all the while; it was the outcry that faded, as portrait studios filled with customers.
